profile.title: IBAMA infraction notices (Autos de Infração), Brazil

series.notices: Number of infraction notices issued in the month (non-cancelled)
series.fine_total_brl: Total value of fines issued in the month (non-cancelled), in Reais: values in earlier currencies are converted at the official rate of each currency reform (no inflation adjustment)

categories.PDC: Policy-Driven Change: legislation, mandate, agency restructuring or political transition
categories.SP: Seasonal Pattern: a recurring annual enforcement cycle
categories.DQE: Data-Quality Event: reporting failure, system migration, backlog, duplication or retroactive correction
categories.GES: Genuine Enforcement Shift: a real change in enforcement intensity not explained by the above

llm.reasoning: The anomaly in 2024-01 is highly suggestive of a seasonal pattern. The number of notices is significantly below the median of the previous 12 months (67% below). Furthermore, this low value mirrors a pattern observed across numerous previous years (9 out of 10 years since 2014), including several years flagged as anomalous. The fact that the same calendar month has been flagged in multiple years reinforces the seasonal hypothesis. There's no evidence of a policy change (PDC) or a data quality issue (DQE) given the lack of associated events or anomalies in other related series. While the fine_total_brl series also shows a decrease, the notice count is the primary driver of the anomaly. Therefore, Seasonal Pattern (SP) is the most likely explanation.

The anomaly in 2024-01 is highly suggestive of a seasonal pattern. The ratio of the value in January to the median of the previous 12 months (0.11) is significantly low, consistent with observations from previous years (9 out of 10 years). Furthermore, this month was flagged as anomalous in 2020-01 and 2021-01. The other series, ‘notices’, also show a similar trend. While there were no policy-driven events or data quality issues evident from the provided records, the consistent low value in January across multiple years strongly indicates a seasonal pattern. The fact that the same calendar month was flagged in other years further reinforces this conclusion.

The anomaly in 2021-01 is highly suggestive of a seasonal pattern. The ratio of notices to the median of the previous 12 months (0.37) is exceptionally low, and has been consistent across 10 of the previous 12 years. Furthermore, the same calendar month was flagged as anomalous in multiple prior years (1983-01, 1989-01, 1996-01, 1999-01, 2003-01, 2009-01, 2010-01, 2012-01, 2014-01, 2017-01, 2019-01, 2024-01). A Page-Hinkley test found no sustained level shift. While the fine_total_brl series also shows a fluctuation, the core issue is the drastically reduced number of notices, aligning with the historical seasonal pattern. The other detectors (zscore, mad) also support this interpretation. Therefore, Seasonal Pattern (SP) is the most appropriate category.

The anomaly in 2021-01 is consistent with a historical pattern observed across multiple years (9 of 10 years). The ratio to the median is significantly low (-88%), and this direction of deviation (below 1) has been common in previous January months. The fact that it was flagged by multiple detectors (zscore, mad, iforest) and the ensemble score supports the anomaly. While there's no clear policy event, the repeated seasonal pattern and the detection by multiple algorithms point to a genuine enforcement shift. The other series, ‘notices’, also increased in this month, which could be related to the enforcement activity.

The anomaly in 2020-01 is highly suggestive of a seasonal pattern. The ratio of the fine total to the median of the previous 12 months is 0.25, which is far below the median. Crucially, this same calendar month has deviated significantly below the median in 9 out of the last 10 years. The fact that the same month was flagged as anomalous in 1989-01, 1999-01, 2014-01, 2021-01 and 2024-01 strengthens this hypothesis. The COVID-19 pandemic (2020-03) occurred two months later, so it's unlikely to be the primary driver. The records show a normal volume of notices and no significant data quality issues. Therefore, a seasonal pattern is the most plausible explanation.

The anomaly in 2019-01 is strongly indicative of a genuine enforcement shift (GES). The consistent negative deviation in this month across multiple years (10 of 10) combined with detection by multiple anomaly detectors (zscore, MAD, iforest, ensemble) and a sustained level shift identified by the Page-Hinkley test, points to a real change in enforcement intensity. The recent change of federal administration (2019-01) and the addition of an environmental conciliation stage (2019-04) provide plausible context for this shift. While the low notice count is unusual, the historical pattern and the detection methods strongly favor a genuine change in enforcement rather than a seasonal or data-related event.

The anomaly in 2017-01 is highly suggestive of a seasonal pattern. The ratio to the median of the previous 12 months (0.33) is significantly below the median, and this has happened in 10 of the 10 years examined. Furthermore, the same calendar month was flagged as anomalous in multiple prior years, including 2019-01, 2021-01 and 2024-01. There is no evidence of a policy change or a data quality event. The records themselves show no immediate problems (no cancelled notices, no missing identifiers). The Page-Hinkley test did not detect a sustained level shift. Therefore, the most plausible explanation is a genuine seasonal pattern.

The anomaly in 2014-01 is primarily driven by a seasonal pattern. The number of notices is significantly below the median of the previous 12 months (66% reduction), and this deviation is consistent with historical data across numerous years (9 out of 10 years in the past show a similar low value for January). The fact that the same month was flagged as anomalous in multiple years (including 2024-01) strengthens this seasonal interpretation. While the fine total also decreased, the focus here is on the notice count. The absence of a sustained level shift (Page-Hinkley test) further supports a cyclical pattern rather than a systematic change. The other series flagged in the same month (fine_total_brl) may be related to this seasonal shift.

The anomaly in 2014-01 is significantly below the median of the previous 12 months, and this deviation has occurred in 9 of the 10 years examined. The ratio to the previous 12 months is 0.15, indicating a substantial decrease. Furthermore, the same calendar month has been flagged as anomalous in multiple years (1989, 1999, 2020, 2021, 2024). Given the seasonality check, the anomaly is consistently below the median across years. While there’s no sustained level shift detected by the Page-Hinkley test, the recurring nature of this anomaly points strongly towards a seasonal pattern (SP). The other series, notices, also show a high number of cancellations in the same month, reinforcing the seasonal interpretation.

The anomaly in 2012-01 is consistent with a historical seasonal pattern. The ratio to the median of the previous 12 months (0.49) is significantly below the median, and this has occurred in 8 of the 10 years prior to 2012. Furthermore, the same month has been flagged as anomalous in numerous other years, including 2019-01, 2021-01 and 2024-01. No sustained level shift was detected using the Page-Hinkley test, and no other series were flagged in the same month. The New Forest Code introduced in 2012 may have influenced enforcement, but the established historical pattern strongly suggests a seasonal effect (SP).

The anomaly in 2011-11 is driven by a significantly elevated fine total compared to the median of the previous 12 months (3.33x). While this is above the seasonal pattern as observed over the past 10 years (7 out of 10 years showed an increase), there's no clear seasonal pattern. The data does not indicate a policy-driven event, as the new Forest Code event is 6 months after the anomaly. The records show no data quality issues, such as a burst of cancellations or missing identifiers. Therefore, a genuine enforcement shift seems the most plausible explanation.

The anomaly in 2010-01 is characterized by a significant drop in notices (59% reduction) compared to the median of the previous 12 months. Critically, this month has been flagged as anomalous in multiple years (8 of 10), and the ratio to the previous 12 months is consistently low. The Page-Hinkley test confirms a sustained level shift within 2 months, suggesting a persistent change. Given these factors, a seasonal pattern (SP) is the most plausible explanation, as the deviation is replicated across multiple years and calendar months. While policy changes (PDC) are possible, there's no specific event identified within the timeframe that could explain this drop. Data quality issues (DQE) are less likely given the consistent pattern. A genuine enforcement shift (GES) is the least likely explanation due to the lack of broader systemic changes.

The anomaly in 2009-01 is highly suggestive of a seasonal pattern (SP). The ratio to the median of previous 12 months is a dramatic -64%, and this has occurred in 8 out of 10 years. Furthermore, the same calendar month has been flagged as anomalous in many other years, including 1983, 1989, 1996, 1999, 2003, 2010, 2012, 2014, 2017, 2019, 2021, and 2024. The Page-Hinkley test confirms a sustained level shift within two months. While a new decree was introduced in 2008, this is unlikely to be the root cause given the long history of this anomaly. The large drop in notices is consistent with a seasonal decline. There are no other series flagged in the same month, ruling out other immediate causes.

The anomaly in 2008-06 is primarily driven by a seasonal pattern. The 2008-06 anomaly was also flagged by multiple detectors (zscore, MAD, ensemble score). The introduction of a new decree in July 2008 (policy-driven) occurring only one month after the anomaly, doesn’t explain the magnitude of the increase. The data quality indicators (no cancelled notices, no missing IDs) also don’t suggest a data issue. Therefore, the strongest explanation is a seasonal pattern.

Therefore, a genuine enforcement shift (GES) is the most plausible explanation.

The anomaly in 2003-01 is driven by a significant seasonal pattern. The ratio to the previous 12 months (0.39) is exceptionally low, and this is a recurring event across multiple years (7 out of 10). The relatively low number of cancelled notices and records without identifiers in this period is also not indicative of a data quality issue. Given the substantial increase and persistent anomalies across multiple years, a genuine enforcement shift (GES) is the most plausible explanation. A policy change (PDC) is less likely given the lack of supporting events. A data quality event (DQE) is unlikely due to the sustained level shift and the fact that other series are also affected.

The fact that the same month was flagged in multiple years, including 1983-01, 1989-01, and 1999-01, suggests a more persistent issue than a simple seasonal pattern. Given the lack of a clear policy event and the presence of a sustained level shift, a genuine enforcement shift (GES) is the most plausible explanation, though data quality issues (DQE) cannot be entirely ruled out given the large increase and the presence of cancelled notices and missing identifiers in the surrounding months. The anomaly in 1994-07 is driven by a massive increase in fines (5852% relative to the median) and a significant shift in the data series' behavior compared to the previous years. The anomaly in 1993-08 is driven by a massive increase in the number of infraction notices (287 vs. median of 62) and a significant spike in the total fine value (17,367 BRL vs. median of 1,063 BRL). The seasonality check reveals that August consistently shows a high ratio compared to the median of its previous 12 months, occurring in 7 of the 10 years examined. Furthermore, a sustained level shift was detected within 2 months. The concurrent spike in fine_total_brl, coupled with the currency reform implemented in August 1993, strongly suggests a policy-driven change. The currency reform would have dramatically increased the monetary value of fines, explaining the dramatic shift in the data.

The anomaly in 1993-08 is driven by a massive increase in fines (17,367 BRL vs. median of 357 BRL). This is amplified by the fact that the same calendar month (August) deviated in the same direction (above 1) in 9 of the 10 years prior. Furthermore, a Page-Hinkley test indicated a sustained level shift within 2 months. Crucially, the month is flagged as anomalous by multiple detectors (zscore, iforest, ensemble). The most likely explanation is a policy-driven change: the currency reform in August 1993, where the Cruzeiro was replaced by the Cruzeiro Real, would have dramatically affected the reported fine values, which were previously in Cruzeiro. The sudden jump in fines is consistent with this event. The other series, notices, also shows a significant increase.

The anomaly in 1993-02 is characterized by a significant drop in the number of notices (60% below the median) and a relatively low value. The anomaly in 1992-04 is characterized by a massive increase in fines (320 vs. median of 19) within a single month. Seasonality analysis reveals that this month has historically shown elevated values, with a ratio above 1 in 6 of the preceding 10 years. While there is no sustained level shift (Page-Hinkley test), the data records show a burst of notices (133) in April 1992, with a high fine total, and a few cancellations. There were no events to explain this, and no other series were flagged in the same month. Given the strong seasonal component and the magnitude of the change, a genuine enforcement shift (GES) is the most plausible explanation. The data doesn't suggest a policy change (PDC) or a data quality issue (DQE).

The anomaly is most likely due to a Genuine Enforcement Shift (GES). The July 1989 notice count (364) represents a 4.02x increase over the median of the previous 12 months (90), which is a significant deviation. While the seasonality check shows a tendency for July to be above average, this is only true in 5 out of 7 years, and the magnitude of the increase is far greater than any of those previous years. Furthermore, the Page-Hinkley test confirms a sustained level shift. The key event is the creation of IBAMA in February 1989, coinciding with the spike in notices. While the currency reform in January 1989 could theoretically influence fine values, the number of notices is not directly related to monetary changes. The fact that the anomaly was not flagged in any other year strengthens the argument for a genuine shift in enforcement activity following the agency's establishment.

The anomaly in 1989-03 is highly suggestive of a genuine enforcement shift (GES). The month's notice count is significantly below the median and has been consistently low for the previous years, with several other months in the same calendar period also flagged as anomalous. The Page-Hinkley test confirms a sustained level shift. Crucially, the timing coincides with the creation of IBAMA (1989-02) and a significant currency reform (1989-01) which could have influenced enforcement strategies or reporting practices. The ensemble score (0.41) is below the threshold, further suggesting a genuine shift rather than a data quality event. The fact that this month was flagged in 1981-03 and 1996-03 adds weight to the possibility of a sustained change.

The anomaly in 1989-01 is highly suggestive of a policy-driven change (PDC). The massive increase in fines (19489% above the median) coincides with a significant currency reform implemented in January 1989. The Plano Verao was a monetary reform that replaced the Cruzado with the Cruzado Novo. This reform likely led to a change in the way fines were calculated and reported, causing a surge in the total value. The other flagged anomalous months (1999-01, 2014-01, 2020-01, 2021-01, 2024-01) also appear to be linked to policy changes. The Page-Hinkley test confirms a sustained level shift within 2 months, further supporting this interpretation. While seasonality could play a role, the extreme magnitude of the change and the timing relative to the currency reform strongly indicate a policy-driven cause.

The anomaly in 1988-12 is highly suggestive of a seasonal pattern.
